newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair says Major weak and vacillating.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair says Major weak and vacillating.

text.p: Labour opposition leader Tony Blair on Saturday accused Prime Minister John Major of being the weak and vacillating leader of a government paralysed by faction fighting.
Blair, making his last major speech to party activists before the election that must be called by May, urged Major: "Stop the dithering. Name the day. Call the General Election."
With voter surveys showing Major more popular than the Conservative Party he heads, Blair went on the offensive with one of the most withering attacks on his arch-opponent.
"In an uncertain world Britain cannot afford an uncertain Prime Minister," said Blair whose party holds a 15-20 percent lead in opinion polls.

He said the Conservative government, bedevilled by mutinies over Britain's role in the European Union, was paralysed by faction fighting. "The Tory (Conservative) Party is not led at at all," he said.

"Government is nothing more than a propaganda machine," he told the Labour party's local government conference in the central English town of Nottingham. Party activists gave him a standing ovation as he delivered his pre-election rallying cry.
He accused Major of mishandling the crisis over mad cow disease and dithering with a series of conflicting messages over whether Britain will join a European single currency.
Blair, bidding to lead his party out of 18 years in the political wilderness, indicated that education would become a major political battleground in the election campaign.
He pledged to raise standards in British schools by promising to plough into education the money saved by getting people off welfare.
"Remember that pledge. Less spent on the costs of unemployment. More spent in schools to give our children the future they need. That's The New Labour Way," he told activists.

Blair also singled out for praise "the tenacity and brilliance" of his left-wing education spokesman David Blunkett, who on Friday backed away from ambitions to abolish grammar schools that select their pupils according to ability.

The centrist Blair has sought to modernise the old working-class image of Labour by shedding much socialist dogma in the search for middle class backing to stop the Conservatives winning their fifth election victory in a row.
